overview.summary: Graphic designers create visual material, such as logos, posters, websites, packaging and social media graphics, that communicates a message clearly.
overview.problems: They help organizations and people explain ideas, attract attention and look consistent and professional.
overview.worksWith: Clients, marketing teams, writers, printers and other designers, and developers on web projects.
overview.workplaces: Design studios, advertising and marketing companies, in-house teams, publishers, and freelance or remote work.

timeline.title: Read the brief
timeline.description: The designer goes through the client's request: the audience, the message, the size and the deadline.
timeline.why: A good design solves a specific communication problem.

timeline.title: Sketching and exploring ideas
timeline.description: The designer sketches, makes mood boards and tries different layouts, colours and fonts.
timeline.why: Trying many options leads to better final ideas.

timeline.title: Designing in software
timeline.description: The designer builds the chosen idea in design software, adjusts spacing, text and images, and checks that it works at different sizes.
timeline.why: Small details of alignment and readability make the difference between clear and confusing.

timeline.title: Getting feedback and revising
timeline.description: The designer presents the work to a client or colleague, takes their feedback and revises the design.
timeline.why: Designs usually change after feedback, and that is a normal part of the job.

timeline.title: Preparing files
timeline.description: The designer exports the files in the right formats and sizes for print or screen.
timeline.why: A great design can fail if the files are prepared wrongly.

timeline.title: Tight deadlines and last-minute changes
timeline.description: Clients sometimes ask for changes close to a deadline.
timeline.why: Design work often runs to fixed launch or print dates.

responsibilities: Understanding the client's goals and audience
Preparing files correctly for print or screen
challenges: Feedback can be subjective, and clients may want changes you do not agree with.
Deadlines are tight and last-minute edits are common.
Competition is strong, especially for freelance work.
Income can be irregular for freelancers.
The work involves long hours at a screen.
Building a portfolio takes time, and it often matters more than qualifications.
workEnvironment: Mostly desk and computer based, in studios, offices or from home. The work is a mix of independent design time and meetings with clients or teams. Freelancers manage their own time and clients.
rewards: Flexibility, including freelance or remote work in some roles
A portfolio that shows what you can do
tradeoffs: Pay and demand that vary by country and employer

activity.title: Redesign a poster for a school event
steps: Pick a real or imaginary event and list the key facts: what, when and where.
Sketch three different layouts on paper.
Choose one and make it with a free design tool such as Canva, or by hand.
Show it to two people and ask what they noticed first and whether the key facts are clear.
Revise it once based on their feedback.
activity.outcome: You practise clear visual communication and using feedback to improve a design.
activity.safety: Use only images you own or that are free to use, and avoid putting personal details such as home addresses on anything you share.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
